title: The good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37)
hookLine: a priest and a Levite pass by, and the despised foreigner stops
tomorrow: the lost sheep and the lost coin

cards: A scholar of the Law stands up to test Jesus. What must I do to have eternal life? Jesus turns it back: what does the Law say?
The man answers well: love God with all your heart, soul, strength and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself. Right, says Jesus. Do this, and you'll live.
But the man wants to know where the edges are. In the Douay-Rheims: "And who is my neighbour?" Who counts, and who doesn't?
It's a question about where love is allowed to stop. Jesus doesn't give him a definition. He tells him a story.

teach.b: A man is going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, through lonely country, and he falls among robbers. He's stripped, beaten and left half dead. A priest comes down the road, sees him, and passes by on the other side.
A Levite, who served in the Temple, does the same.
The story never says why. People have guessed for centuries; Jesus doesn't tell us, and he doesn't need to. Then a Samaritan comes.
To the people listening, a Samaritan was a neighbor from across a long and bitter religious divide.
And this one, Luke says, is moved with compassion. The Greek word comes from the gut, a feeling in your insides.

He pours oil and wine on the man's wounds, bandages them, puts him on his own animal, takes him to an inn, and pays for his care: two pence, the Douay-Rheims says, and a promise to cover anything more.
Then Jesus asks the scholar: "Which of these three, in thy opinion, was neighbour to him that fell among the robbers?" Notice what happened.

teach.h: NOT WHO IS, BUT WHO PROVED NEIGHBOR.
teach.b: The man asked, who is my neighbor, who do I have to love? Jesus answers a different question: who acted like a neighbor? The scholar doesn't say the word Samaritan.
He says: the one who showed him mercy.

teach.h: GO, AND DO THOU IN LIKE MANNER.
teach.b: And Jesus says: "Go, and do thou in like manner." Early Church writers also read the story another way: Christ as the Samaritan, the wounded man as all of us, the inn as the Church.
Pope Francis gave a whole chapter of his letter Fratelli Tutti to this road.

how: Catholics hear this parable at Sunday Mass and in teaching on the works of mercy; Pope Francis's encyclical Fratelli Tutti gives a chapter to it, and some Catholic hospitals and charities take the Samaritan as their model.

games.q: you're a scholar of the Law. you ask Jesus, who is my neighbor? what does he do?
o: give you a clear list of who counts.
tell you a story and ask who acted like a neighbor.
tell you everyone is your neighbor and move on.
games.why: he tells the story of the man on the Jericho road, then asks who proved neighbor. and he ends: “Go, and do thou in like manner.”

practice: Think about the roads you'll walk today, the hallways, the streets, the feeds, and who's lying by the side of them: not always bleeding, sometimes just lonely, or overwhelmed, or ignored.

Picture one person you usually pass by on the other side, then picture stopping; what would it cost you, ten minutes, a little awkwardness? If you pray, you can ask for the Samaritan's gut-deep compassion.

wordCard.voice: Samaritan. A stranger from across a bitter divide, the one who stopped and showed mercy on the Jericho road.

orig.note: Greek: he was moved with compassion, from splanchna, the inward parts, the gut.
